clue.text: Text: 'Boris finally gets Conservative trip arranged'

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word it follows, so only its end is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the prime minister's first name

indicators.note: something arranged has been put into a new order, so these letters are set out afresh

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
taken as written, then shuffled

explanation.surface: A satirical headline about Boris Johnson's party organising a trip for him.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon and quotation marks make 'Text' look like a label for a quoted headline, but it is the definition; the rest builds S, C and a rearranged TRIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A script is the written words of a play or speech, so it is a kind of text.

clue.text: Faith's bloody gate-crashing company

indicators.note: a gate-crasher forces their way inside an event, so one piece pushes into the middle of another

parts.note: Co is the usual abbreviation for company
blood is red, so bloody suggests that colour

explanation.surface: Someone named Faith is swearing about a firm that turned up uninvited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faith's' reads as a woman's name with a possessive, but it is the definition followed by 'is' as the link; 'bloody' is a colour, not an expletive.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a statement of religious belief, from the Latin for 'I believe', so it names a faith.

clue.text: Which is to say, grabbing member at a ball amounts to obstruction

indicators.note: to grab is to hold something tightly in your grip, so one piece clasps another inside it

parts.note: i.e. abbreviates the Latin id est, 'that is to say'
an MP is a Member of Parliament
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A politician groping someone at a ball, framed as an obstruction charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member' hints at something cruder in this surface, but it is a Member of Parliament; 'at' simply joins the abbreviation to the event.
explanation.definitionFit: Impedance is the act or quality of hindering progress, the noun from impede, so it is a synonym of obstruction.

clue.text: Swell all round organ and remove a bit

indicators.note: going all round something means surrounding it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a swell is an old word for a smartly dressed upper-class man, a toff in British slang
the ear is an organ of hearing

explanation.surface: Something swelling around a body part that needs a bit cut away, like minor surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' looks like a verb about puffing up, but it is the noun: a toff, a posh British gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: To tear off is to rip a piece away from something larger, so it means removing a part.

clue.text: Digger recruiting daughter as bodyguard

indicators.note: recruiting means taking someone into your ranks, so one piece is taken inside another

parts.note: a miner digs for coal or ore
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A labourer hiring his daughter to protect him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digger' could be an Australian soldier or an excavator; here it is a miner.
explanation.definitionFit: Minder is British slang for a personal protector, someone paid to look after a celebrity or criminal.

clue.text: Lott, terribly into the drink, gets blotchy

indicators.note: going into something puts it inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: the drink is slang for the sea, here the Mediterranean, the Med

indicators.note: something done terribly is done in a mess, so these letters come out jumbled

parts.note: the surname taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A man named Lott, hitting the bottle badly, ends up with a blotchy face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the drink' suggests alcohol, but in crosswords it is often the sea; here the Mediterranean, abbreviated Med.
explanation.definitionFit: Mottled skin or stone is marked with irregular patches of colour, exactly what blotchy describes.

clue.text: Niche-like sex

definitions.meaning: first meaning: full of or resembling a nook, a small recess
second meaning: British slang for sexual activity

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is built as nook plus -y, an adjective; the second is a jokey slang noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A nook is a small recess like a niche, while the slang noun is a playful word for lovemaking.

clue.text: Burnt-out UKIP leader hated sex romps

indicators.note: romping is boisterous unruly play, so these letters tumble into a new order
a leader comes at the front, so only the opening letter of the party name is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the party's name
taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A worn-out UKIP leader who disliked sex scandals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'romps' sounds like the noun from tabloid 'sex romps', but it works as a verb telling the letters to run about. UKIP is the UK Independence Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone burnt-out has used up all their energy, so they are completely drained and tired.

clue.text: (& 19dn.) Belated "Nix!" or other possible consequence of Leave vote?

indicators.note: other means different in form, so these letters take on a new arrangement

parts.note: three words taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A late refusal, or some other outcome, following Britain's vote to leave the European Union.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans 8 and 19 down. 'Nix!' looks like an exclamation of refusal, but its letters are simply fodder alongside 'Belated' and 'or'.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaving the European Union without any agreed withdrawal terms was a feared possible outcome of the 2016 referendum.

clue.text: (& 12/21/26ac.) Pay heed, readers — don't fold back your organs

definitions.meaning: first meaning: stay alert and watchful

definitions.text: readers — don't fold back your organs
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an instruction to Private Eye readers not to fold shut their copies of the magazine, an organ being a periodical

explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans 9, 12, 21 and 26 across. 'organs' looks like body parts, but it means publications: this crossword's readers hold copies of Private Eye, so their 'Eyes' should stay unfolded.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom urging someone to stay vigilant and watchful, which is what paying heed means.

clue.text: Support right in a forlorn hope — sign of lack of character?

explanation.surface: Backing the right side in a lost cause, which might suggest someone lacking moral fibre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' looks like moral fibre, but it means a letter: the punctuation mark stands where letters are missing, as in don't.
explanation.definitionFit: This punctuation mark indicates omitted letters in contractions, so it signals that a typographic character is absent.

clue.text: Loathe Lords dismissing southern pathetic Remoaners notion of 8/19?

indicators.note: something pathetic is feeble and in a poor state, so these letters are reworked
to dismiss is to send away, so a letter is dropped from the word

the plural noun minus its southern letter

explanation.surface: Hating the House of Lords, with their feeble Remainers' view of a no-deal Brexit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remoaners' is a Brexiteer insult for Remain supporters who kept complaining; 'pathetic' seems to describe them but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Remain supporters saw leaving without an agreement as a path to disaster, echoing the proverb about good intentions.

explanation.walkthrough: 'load of gas' suggests empty talk, but it is a full tank of fuel.

clue.text: Mildly pissed females going topless — good sign?

indicators.note: losing the top means losing what comes first in a down answer, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: happy is a euphemism for slightly drunk

explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' sounds like a nightclub scene, but it means removing the first letter of WOMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: An omen is a portent of what is to come, and a happy one foretells good fortune.

clue.text: Want date to get the dirt

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for date
earth is soil, dirt

explanation.surface: Someone wanting a date in order to dig up gossip about them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want' reads as a verb meaning desire, but it is the noun meaning lack; 'the dirt' looks like gossip but is soil.
explanation.definitionFit: Want in the sense of scarcity or shortage matches a dearth, a lack of something needed.

clue.text: American lump debts getting go-ahead

parts.note: Am. is an abbreviation for American

IOUs are written promises to repay, so debts

explanation.definitionFit: A go-ahead person or company is enterprising and eager to succeed, which is what ambitious means.

clue.text: "Get fat" ranch

definitions.meaning: first meaning: grow wider, as in middle-age widening of the waistline
second meaning: American term for a large farm or estate

explanation.definitionFit: To widen out is to grow broader at the waist, and in American English the noun names a large cattle property.

clue.text: Street-wise way of saying the newspapers are getting people low

definitions.note: a verb phrase; the answer is the base verb, meaning to make people low

indicators.note: street speech is how something is pronounced in casual urban talk, so we go by its spoken form

explanation.surface: A streetwise remark that the newspapers are bringing everyone down.
explanation.walkthrough: In slangy street talk 'the' is pronounced 'de', so 'the press' comes out as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To depress someone is to make them sad and dispirited, bringing their mood down.

clue.text: Interferer, active and stiff

a stiff is slang for a corpse, a dead body

explanation.definitionFit: A busybody meddles in other people's affairs, so an interferer is a direct synonym.

clue.text: "One is Charles' mother (ail badly, but that's of no consequence)"

parts.note: one is, in the first person, is I am, contracted

parts.note: mater is Latin for mother, used by the British upper classes
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: The royal 'one' musing that the Queen being unwell does not matter much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One is' mimics royal speech; read plainly it is 'I'm'. Charles is now king, and 'mater' is the posh public-school word for mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Something immaterial is irrelevant and unimportant, so it is of no consequence.

clue.text: see 9ac.
